title: Mohnish Pabrai’s session with YPO’s Mosaic Chapter on  March 20, 2024
summary: A tribute conversation about Charlie Munger held shortly after his memorial, framed around 'take a simple idea and take it seriously.' Pabrai explains why cloning is his central edge (Tom Peters' gas stations, Microsoft, Sam Walton, Costco), how Munger moved Buffett from Graham-style bargains to great businesses at fair prices, Munger's mental models (reciprocation without a calibration engine), his subtle board influence at Costco, the no-called-strikes view of his Turkey investments, and stories of Munger's win-win integrity, humor, and giving nature.

ideas.idea: Take a simple idea and take it seriously: an aha nugget of wisdom that others underweight can become a tremendous competitive advantage if you go all in and fight the status quo.
ideas.detail: Buffett and Munger's success came from the dogged pursuit of a few very simple ideas; it is not enough to read an idea and be impressed, you have to act on it.

ideas.idea: Humans have an aversion to cloning, and the small sliver of master cloners owns the world; forcing himself to copy smart things gave him a big edge.
ideas.detail: At about 20 he read Tom Peters' story of two California gas stations where one owner randomly washed windshields for free, won business, and the competitor never copied it even while losing share. Pabrai set out to prove Peters wrong and after nearly 40 years concluded Peters was mostly right: even handed all your trade secrets, competitors won't change behavior.

ideas.idea: Almost everything at Microsoft is cloned and its research labs have produced nothing, yet it is ahead; Sam Walton and Costco's Jim Sinegal were also master cloners.
ideas.detail: Microsoft copied Lotus for Excel, WordPerfect for Word, the Mac for Windows, and now partners with OpenAI on work Google did. Sinegal, asked what he learned from Sol Price, said it was the wrong question because everything he knows came from Sol Price.

ideas.idea: See's Candies stunned Buffett with its pricing power: raising prices about 10% a year against 3-4% inflation while unit volume kept rising, which became fundamental to Berkshire.
ideas.detail: They paid three times book in the 1970s thinking it was too much, left management alone, and Buffett reset prices every January 1st. Neither understood brands beforehand but became ardent students of the phenomenon and applied it elsewhere.

ideas.idea: Ben Franklin is worth overdosing on: he sold his business in his early forties for a share of future profits to gain independence of thought and action, which is exactly the independence Munger sought.
ideas.detail: Pabrai recommends Walter Isaacson's Franklin biography. Munger wanted financial independence not for Ferraris but to say and do whatever he thought, joking that he 'overshot a bit.' Buffett said Newton was the smartest human but Franklin the wisest, and would question Newton about losing his fortune in the South Sea bubble.

ideas.idea: Munger moved Buffett from Graham's depression-era bargain hunting to buying good businesses at fair prices, and did it by letting Buffett come over at his own pace without criticism.
ideas.detail: Buffett's 2024 letter calls Munger the architect and himself the general contractor. Munger observed an inverse correlation between how difficult a business is and how much money it makes, told Buffett buying Berkshire Hathaway was a big mistake, and never rubbed it in when Buffett's deeply embedded bargain hunter resurfaced.

ideas.idea: Munger improved every institution he touched, including three decades on Costco's board, so subtly that they think the ideas were their own.
ideas.detail: At the March 10 memorial Jim Sinegal could not name anything different at Costco because of Munger, which Pabrai attributes to Munger's finesse in pushing long-term thinking and the mindset that Costco is a buying agent for the customer, not a retailer. Harvard-Westlake, UCSB, Stanford and Michigan also improved.

ideas.idea: Munger read 200-500 books a year and had 50-100 mental models etched in his brain, and could instantly correlate the three that applied to any problem.
ideas.detail: Buffett said Munger had the best mind for analyzing any business, mainly because he got to a 'no' for at least one good reason very quickly, removing noise from his life. Pabrai calls himself a juvenile practitioner and Munger the Kung Fu master.

ideas.idea: The human reciprocation tendency has no calibration engine, so a small favor generates disproportionate goodwill, which he exploits in fund marketing.
ideas.detail: Reciprocation dates to hunter-gatherers storing meat in neighbors' bellies. Pabrai sends prospective investors a physical package with a nice Cross pen and a book; only 1-2% return it, and a decent share of the rest wire the multi-million minimum: $50 one way, a few million the other.

ideas.idea: Investing has no called strikes, so Munger saying no to Turkey doesn't matter; what matters is never saying yes to something that doesn't work out.
ideas.detail: Munger was instantly negative every time Turkey came up because of the work and trips it would require, but when Pabrai asked how he would lose money on a Turkish Coke bottler, Munger said 'it is going to work.' You can let a thousand good pitches go by.

ideas.idea: Munger's epitaph 'I tried to be useful' was a simple idea taken seriously to the end: he was closing a nonprofit grant the day before he died with no legacy or publicity upside.
ideas.detail: Pabrai's last one-on-one dinner with Munger was exactly a month before his death; Munger joked to a nurse 'I am dying, how about you?' Munger was agnostic and believed this life was it.

ideas.idea: Givers end up owning the world because of the goodwill they generate; Munger was a pure giver who never asked what was in it for him.
ideas.detail: From Adam Grant's Give and Take: givers help without a scorecard, takers only extract, matchers reciprocate exactly. Munger never read it but embodied the giver.

ideas.idea: Doing business win-win rather than transactionally, and making sure the counterparty feels they got the better end, cements trust for a lifetime and creates tailwinds.
ideas.detail: In the 1960s Munger and Rick Guerin bought a bankrupt radiator-sealant business by paying the two aunts full face value (160,000) on notes they could have bought at a discount, and Munger smoothed things over with the mistress-executor at the California Club. Two years later when Guerin offered his half for 200,000, Munger wrote him a check for 300,000.

ideas.idea: Buffett and Munger are gamblers who only bet when the odds are in their favor and never sit at a Vegas table.
ideas.detail: Buffett joked he wanted to be a bookie but his parents disapproved, so he went into insurance. Pabrai was banned from an off-strip Las Vegas casino after taking about 150,000 over a few months at blackjack with a non-card-counting system exploiting the casino's thinner house edge; Munger loved the story.

ideas.idea: Munger's wisdom extended to reading and navigating the full spectrum of human personalities, not just polymath knowledge.
ideas.detail: With eight kids and many in-laws and grandkids, he applied different frameworks to different people and loved Franklin's line to keep your eyes wide open before marriage and half shut afterward.

ideas.idea: Reading and rereading the 11 speeches in Poor Charlie's Almanack, especially The Psychology of Human Misjudgment, is worth more than a four-year college degree.
ideas.detail: Older editions are better because of the illustrations. Understanding how the apparatus between our ears actually functions gives a huge leg up; rereading yearly, Pabrai finds passages that feel new each time.

ideas.idea: Munger gave about half his roughly 2 billion net worth to his eight children in 2010, the one year with no US estate tax, and focused on giving the rest away.
ideas.detail: Each child received about 125 million in Berkshire stock, now worth roughly 400 million, and they have done impressive and varied philanthropic work. He likely still had a couple of billion at death.
